figures.caption: Figure 10.2.2 shows the circuit implementation of the analog computer proposed in Fig. 10.2.1. Active-RC integrators are employed due to their superior dynamic range. An RC calibration circuit adjusts the integrator gain, which is proportional to the RC product, by tuning the capacitors in the op-amp feedback paths. The op-amps are implemented with two-stage differential amplifiers to drive the resistive load. Since each integrator has –90O phase shift, I and Q signals are available at the output of the integrators. The modulator is implemented at base-band to preclude image issues in the transmitter up-conversion path. In a Bluetooth implementation, the input of the modulator consists of a stream of random binary data shaped by a Gaussian filter. The linearity requirement of the multipliers is relaxed considering that a Gaussian function has the same mathematical form in time domain as its Fourier transform [4]. The multipliers, implemented as 4-FET switches, receive a digital clock at 1Mb/s as shown in Fig. 10.2.2. The data edges are first aligned with the 12MHz system clock, and a logic circuit produces complementary clock signals to drive the 4-FET switches. An analog Gaussian low-pass filter following the modulator serves two purposes. First, it produces the desired GFSK spectrum. Second, it removes the glitches created in the multipliers. The low-pass filter incorporates a 4th-order active–RC design with a 3-dB bandwidth of 500kHz. To meet the spectrum mask requirements, the modulator output swing must be well defined. Otherwise, the nonlinearity of the upconversion mixers as well as the distortion of the integrators create undesired inter-modulation terms. As illustrated in Fig. 10.2.3,

references.sentence: (2), is realized by an analog computer comprising the three basic analog building blocks, namely, adders, multipliers, and integrators (Fig. 10.2.1).
Figure 10.2.2 shows the circuit implementation of the analog computer proposed in Fig. 10.2.1.
The multipliers, implemented as 4-FET switches, receive a digital clock at 1Mb/s as shown in Fig. 10.2.2.
As illustrated in Fig. 10.2.3, amplifier A, followed by capacitor CA result in a total capacitance of A × CA in parallel with the first integrator resistor.
The amplifier in Fig. 10.2.3 is a Gilbert-type current-steering circuit.
The integrator input connects to the input stage of the amplifier, and gain control signals, VP and VR in Fig. 10.2.3, are applied to the current-steering transistors.
Depicted in Fig. 10.2.4, the squarelaw property of a long channel MOSFET is utilized to realize the power detector.
When the modulator input is set to 1, the transmitter output tone is about 160kHz away from the carrier at 2.45GHz (Fig. 10.2.5).
Figure 10.2.6 shows the transmitter output with pseudo-random data at 1Mb/s applied to the modulator input.
A microphotograph of the device is shown in Fig. 10.2.7.
